claims.text: Applying an ultrathin, dense oxide film by atomic layer deposition enhances the extreme-corrosion resistance of stainless steel.
The corrosion improvement arises because the deposited oxide limits the ingress of corrosive species.
Standard stainless steel has a native passive oxide layer that is relatively fragile.
An ultrathin Al2O3 or similarly stable oxide coating can be deposited on stainless steel by ALD.
High-salinity, acidic, and high-humidity environments can challenge conventional stainless-steel passivation.
The proposed ALD process produces a uniform coating over the steel surface.
The proposed ALD coating is pinhole-free and densely packed.
The ALD-deposited oxide acts as an effective and stable barrier.
The oxide barrier prevents aggressive ions from reaching the metal substrate.
The oxide barrier mitigates localized breakdown of the native passive layer.
ALD-coated stainless steel will exhibit a delayed onset of corrosion relative to unmodified stainless steel.
ALD-coated stainless steel will exhibit a lower corrosion rate relative to unmodified stainless steel.
ALD-coated stainless steel will develop fewer pitting sites relative to unmodified stainless steel.
Coating thickness and adhesion quality may limit the effectiveness and long-term stability of the ALD coating.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the coating and steel substrate may limit long-term coating stability.
The barrier properties of ALD coatings are well documented in similar contexts.
The performance under extreme corrosion conditions and the optimal coating thickness and composition remain to be established empirically.
